analysis.one_liner: Lets US drug buyers sue when manufacturers charge foreign wholesalers far less than American ones.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced: introduced by a single senator with no cosponsors, it sat in the Judiciary Committee until the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: American consumers paid about 43% more for prescription drugs than Canadians, according to the GAO findings cited in the bill. The bill would amend a 1936 antitrust law that bans price discrimination so that selling the same drug to a foreign wholesaler at a much lower price than to a US wholesaler could be challenged as unlawful discrimination. It was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, never got a hearing or a vote, and died when the 106th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: American consumers, especially seniors, who would benefit from legal pressure pushing US drug prices toward the lower prices charged abroad. US wholesalers would gain a legal tool against manufacturers charging them more than foreign wholesalers for the same drugs.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Seniors and other Americans who buy prescription drugs

how_it_helps.text: The bill's findings state that, per the General Accounting Office, American consumers pay on average 43% more for prescription drugs than Canadian consumers, and that many seniors cross the border to buy the same US-made drugs cheaper.

It amends the Robinson-Patman Act so that price discrimination between US wholesalers and foreign wholesalers is deemed to injure competition, giving US buyers a legal cause of action when manufacturers charge much lower prices abroad for the same US-approved drugs.
The bill explicitly declares that principles of fair dealing in pricing, established in US law since 1936, should apply to prescription drug sales to wholesalers in different countries.

analysis.who_pays: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers, which could face lawsuits and pressure to raise foreign prices or lower US prices, reducing the revenue they currently earn from charging Americans more. Consumers abroad could face higher prices if manufacturers narrowed the gap by raising foreign prices instead of cutting US ones.

drawbacks.text: The remedy is indirect: it relies on private antitrust lawsuits, not a price cap or government-set prices, so whether it would actually lower drug prices — and by how much — is uncertain.

The bill itself acknowledges the drug industry's argument in reverse: the US supports drug research through NIH funding, the R&D tax credit, and high domestic prices, and manufacturers could argue that US consumers effectively subsidize the world's new medicines, so narrowing the price gap could come at some cost to research incentives.
If manufacturers responded by raising prices in Canada and other countries rather than lowering US prices, consumers abroad would pay more and the intended benefit to Americans could be blunted.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill targets a real, documented problem — Americans paying roughly 43% more than Canadians for the same drugs — and uses an existing, long-standing antitrust principle rather than price controls. Its main weakness is that litigation is a slow, uncertain lever: any price relief for Americans would depend on lawsuits and market pressure, not an automatic rule, and some of the adjustment could come from higher foreign prices. On balance, the potential gain for seniors and other drug buyers outweighed the speculative cost to research incentives, which the bill's own findings address.

outcome.mechanism: A single senator introduced it, no one else signed on, the Judiciary Committee never acted on it, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Slade Gorton introduced the Prescription Drug Fairness Act in the Senate on April 26, 2000, citing GAO data that Americans pay 43% more than Canadians for prescription drugs.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day.
No further action was taken, and the bill never received a committee mark-up, a floor vote, or House consideration before the 106th Congress ended on January 3, 2001.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Brand-name pharmaceutical manufacturers kept the status quo, in which they face no legal challenge to charging US buyers substantially more than foreign wholesalers for the same drugs. American seniors, who pay the highest drug prices in the industrialized world, gained nothing.

for.name: Slade Gorton
for.role: U.S. Senator from Washington; sole sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 26, 2000 and delivered introductory remarks, framing it as protection for American seniors against foreign drug price discrimination.

sides.party_line_note: A Republican senator sponsored the bill and no other senator, from either party, signed on, so no party pattern can be read from the record; the bill never reached a vote.

industries.note: The bill would let US wholesalers sue when manufacturers charge foreign wholesalers much less for the same US-approved drugs, pressuring manufacturers to narrow the price gap that leaves Americans paying 43% more than Canadians. The bill died with no action, leaving the industry's dual-pricing structure untouched.

Wholesalers would gain a legal cause of action against manufacturers charging them more than foreign wholesalers, a tool they could use to buy cheaper and pass savings on. The bill never became law, so the tool was never created.
